title: Long-Context Attention Benchmark
one_liner: A fair comparison tool showing how different attention speedup methods trade efficiency, mask flexibility, and scalability in training very long sequences.
lead: Attention (the part of a language model that reads relevant context by checking word pairs) gets impossibly slow with a million tokens: the cost grows as the sequence length squared. This paper builds a unified benchmark to fairly compare which speedup methods actually work and where each one breaks.

problem.h2: Why attention grinds to a halt
paras: Attention in a language model works by scoring every word pair: for each of N words as a reader, it computes how relevant each of the other N words is. That is N times N scores, taking time and memory that grow as N squared. A beginner might hope that faster GPUs or more servers just solve this because they would do the checking faster. But the problem is structural: the algorithm requires all N squared pairs to be computed, so even perfect hardware cannot escape this cost.

Researchers have tried two directions. First, kernel-level tricks: accelerate the GPU code that does attention by changing how data flows through memory. Second, spread the work: split a long sequence across multiple GPUs and have them work in parallel, reducing each GPU's workload. But which tricks actually help—and under what conditions—was unclear because each method was tested separately on different hardware and with different mask patterns. Do they work for all kinds of attention masks (rectangular patterns, triangular for causal reading, sparse blocks)? Do they scale to a million tokens? Nobody had built a fair test where all methods competed on identical data.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence:
callout.html: Build one unified benchmark that measures all the major attention speedup methods side-by-side, across different mask patterns and sequence lengths, on clusters up to 96 GPUs.

panels.title: 1. Naive attention: check everything
panels.caption: With N tokens, compute N squared pairs. Time explodes, memory explodes.

panels.title: 2. Two different speedup tactics emerge
panels.viz_args: Tactic A (kernel tricks): code-level speedups. Tactic B (distributed): split across GPUs
panels.caption: Both reduce cost, but how much? Which works where? Unknown.

panels.title: 3. Speedups need different mask shapes
panels.viz_args: Some masks: dense. Some: triangular (causal). Some: sparse blocks.
panels.caption: Each mask shape favors different speedups. Must measure all.

panels.title: 4. Benchmark integrates all the pieces
panels.viz_args: One framework: 12 attention kernels + 5 distributed mechanisms + mask generator + data prep
panels.caption: Fair test across methods, masks, sequence lengths, 96 GPUs.

panels.title: 5. Clear trade-offs emerge
panels.caption: Method X faster but rigid mask. Method Y slower but flexible. Practitioners choose.

steps.text: Gather 12 dense attention kernels (naive, PyTorch fused, FlashAttention, etc.) and 5 sparse ones.
Define mask patterns (dense, triangular, sparse blocks) and realistic input data from public datasets.
Run on clusters up to 96 GPUs, record time and memory cost for each method, mask, sequence length.
Identify which method wins for which scenario: fastest kernel? Most flexible mask? Best scaling?
Show practitioners and researchers which attention speedup to pick based on their constraints.

paras: Before: Attention speedup methods lived in separate papers, tested on different hardware, with different mask patterns. No way to compare fairly.

After: A unified benchmark framework sits in the middle. Every method plugs into the same data interface, the same mask generator, the same distributed setup. Like putting all racing cars on one track.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Time and memory cost under real conditions
hidden.name: latency and memory use per condition
paras: The paper measures how many seconds (or milliseconds) each method takes to process a sequence of a given length, and how much GPU memory it uses. This is not abstract—it is wall-clock time on real hardware (NVIDIA H100 GPUs).

The central point: latency and memory are NOT just properties of a method. They depend on three things working together: which attention method is used, which mask pattern is needed, and whether the computation is on one GPU or spread across many. The benchmark isolates each variable.

heat.caption: Darker means faster (lower latency). Highlights show methods measured under both dense and sparse masks.

reads.html: The paper records the actual time and GPU memory each method uses to process sequences of 64K to 1M tokens, across different mask patterns (dense rectangular, triangular, sparse blocks), on single and multi-GPU setups.

Measurements include throughput (tokens per second), peak memory bandwidth utilization, and scaling efficiency—the fraction of theoretical peak performance achieved when work is spread across multiple GPUs.

mechanism.h2: Why the benchmark reveals real trade-offs
paras: Different speedup methods work in different ways. FlashAttention rewrites the GPU code to compute attention in stages, loading and writing data just once instead of repeatedly. Distributed methods (Ulysses, Ring) slice the long sequence across devices, so each GPU handles a shorter chunk. Sparse attention skips unnecessary pairs by computing importance scores first and only processing the top blocks.

Each approach has a hidden cost. FlashAttention is fast for dense attention but cannot easily handle arbitrary sparse patterns. Distributed methods have communication overhead—GPUs must exchange information about what they computed. Sparse methods need to compute which blocks matter, burning time before the main speedup even starts.

A benchmark that tests only one method on one mask type misses these trade-offs. The unified framework forces every method to handle all three inputs (dense masks, triangular masks, sparse masks) and all three scales (single GPU, 8 GPUs, 96 GPUs). This reveals where each method shines and where it falters.

stages.s: Choose a method (e.g. FlashAttention), a mask (dense or sparse), and a sequence length
Run the kernel or distributed mechanism on the benchmark's standardized input data
Repeat for all combinations of methods, masks, sequence lengths
Compare results: which method wins under which conditions? Where do trade-offs appear?

math.h2: The cost formula: latency changes with all three factors
math.words: Latency equals method cost times mask overhead times GPU coordination cost. Specifically: time = kernel_time per token * sequence length * mask penalty factor * (1 + communication overhead fraction when distributed)
symbols: time in milliseconds to process the sequence, for method i and mask j
base time per token for method i, in microseconds (FlashAttention ~2, Naive ~50)
mask overhead factor (1.0 for dense, 1.2 for sparse, 1.1 for triangular)
how many GPUs are involved as a fraction of 96 (0 for single GPU, 1.0 for full cluster)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario: Process 64K tokens with FlashAttention on dense mask, single GPU.
T_kernel = 2 microseconds per token, L = 64 (thousands), M = 1.0, GPU_fraction = 0.
Scenario: Same task but sparse mask (overhead 1.2x).
Scenario: Same task spread across 8 GPUs (fraction 8/96 = 0.083).
latency = 2 * 64 * 1.0 * (1 + 0.1 * 0.083) = 130 milliseconds. Small GPU communication cost.

math.note: Real GPU latency depends on hardware, data layout, and cache behavior, but this formula shows the real pattern: time scales linearly with sequence length and mask rigidity, and suffers only if distributed communication dominates.

bars.h2: Method comparison on 512K-token dense attention, single GPU

charts.title: Kernel speed (latency in ms)
charts.note: Naive is standard Python loops. FlashAttention saves 10-12x by reordering memory access. cuDNN and Flex are close competitors.

charts.title: Same task on sparse (80% masked out) blocks
charts.note: FlashAttention stays expensive (it was built for dense). Dedicated sparse kernels cut cost from 280ms to 60-70ms. Trade-off: sparse kernels need pre-computed importance scores.

items.html: Before a sparse method can skip unimportant pairs, it must compute an importance score for every block. On smaller sequences or low sparsity this scoring cost overwhelms the speedup. The paper shows sparse kernels are fast only when sparsity is above 70-80%.

Spreading attention across 96 GPUs requires GPUs to send data to each other. On slower networks or when sequence length is moderate (64K), the time to shuffle data across the cluster exceeds the speedup. Distributed methods win only at 512K+ tokens.

FlashAttention is optimized for dense rectangular attention. Causal masks (triangular, used when generating tokens one at a time from left to right) add 20-30% overhead. Arbitrary sparse patterns are even costlier. A method fast on one mask may be slow on another.
The paper tests every method on identical hardware and data. No hand-tuned configurations that favor one method. This reveals real-world trade-offs, not benchmark gaming.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small version of the benchmark: take two attention methods (e.g. naive PyTorch and FlashAttention), two mask patterns (dense and sparse), and three sequence lengths (8K, 64K, 256K). Run each combination on a single GPU and record the time in milliseconds. This will show how efficient methods like FlashAttention keep time from growing as fast, while naive methods get exponentially slower, because the optimization reuses memory whereas naive access must fetch and write repeatedly.
demo.metric_eq: speedup = time_naive / time_method (should grow with sequence length for efficient methods)
demo.closing: The demo must show that FlashAttention's speedup (10-12x over naive) grows with sequence length, while sparse attention speedup (5-8x) appears only when the mask is genuinely sparse. Practitioners can then choose based on their constraints.
